'''Keiji Morokuma''' (諸熊 奎治, ''Morokuma Keiji''; July 12, 1934 – November 27, 2017) was a Japanese theoretical chemist and chemical engineer known for developing energy decomposition analysis for molecular interactions<ref>{{Citation |last1=Morokuma |first1=Keiji |chapter=Energy Decomposition Analysis of Molecular Interactions |date=1981 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4757-9634-6_10 |title=Chemical Applications of Atomic and Molecular Electrostatic Potentials |pages=215–242 |editor-last=Politzer |editor-first=Peter |access-date=2023-10-27 |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-9634-6_10 |isbn=978-1-4757-9636-0 |last2=Kitaura |first2=Kazuo |editor2-last=Truhlar |editor2-first=Donald G.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the [[ONIOM]] method in [[quantum chemistry]].<ref name=angchem>{{Cite journal |last1=Cui |first1=Qiang |last2=Irle |first2=Stephan |last3=Musaev |first3=Jamal |date=2018-02-23 |title=Keiji Morokuma (1934–2017) |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |language=en |volume=57 |issue=9 |pages=2288–2289 |doi=10.1002/anie.201800390 |issn=1433-7851|doi-access=free |pmid=29392802 |bibcode=2018ACIE...57.2288C }}</ref><ref name=jpca>{{Cite journal |last1=Bowman |first1=Joel M. |last2=Musaev |first2=Jamal |last3=Nakatsuji |first3=Hiroshi |date=2018-02-01 |title=Keiji Morokuma |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A |language=en |volume=122 |issue=4 |pages=880–881 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.8b00070 |issn=1089-5639|doi-access=free |pmid=29385809 |bibcode=2018JPCA..122..880B }}</ref><ref name=IAQMS>{{Cite web |title=Keiji Morokuma, International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science |url=https://www.iaqms.org/members/morokuma.php |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=www.iaqms.org}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Morokuma was born in [[Kagoshima]], [[Kagoshima Prefecture]] and studied engineering at [[Kyoto University]]. As a student of the Nobel laureate [[Kenichi Fukui]], one of the pioneers of quantum chemistry in Japan, at [[Kyoto University]], Morokuma received his doctorate in 1963 in fuel chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-11-21 |title=諸熊奎治氏が死去 計算化学の第一人者、ノーベル賞候補 : 京都新聞 |url=https://www.kyoto-np.co.jp/politics/article/20171204000071 |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=Kyoto News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181121202839/https://www.kyoto-np.co.jp/politics/article/20171204000071 |archive-date=2018-11-21 |language=ja}}</ref> He became research associate at Kyoto University until 1966, when he became a postdoc at [[Harvard University]] with [[Martin Karplus]] working on [[reaction dynamics]] as a Fulbright visiting scholar.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Keiji Morokuma {{!}} Fulbright Scholar Program |url=https://fulbrightscholars.org/grantee/keiji-morokuma |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=fulbrightscholars.org}}</ref> Afterwards, he joined the Department of Chemistry at the [[University of Rochester]] as an assistant professor in 1967 and eventually became a full professor in 1971. He stayed at Rochester until 1976 before moving to the [[Institute for Molecular Science]] in Okazaki, Japan and worked there until 1993. From 1978 to 1993, Morokuma was also the director of the Computer Center at the institute. In 1993, Morokuma moved back to the US and became the [[William Henry Emerson]] Professor of Chemistry at [[Emory University]]. He retired from Emory University in 2006 and traveled back to Japan, where he became a senior research fellow at the Fukui Institute for Fundamental Chemistry in [[Kyoto University]]. He remained in Kyoto until his death in 2017.<ref name=jpca />

Morokuma developed the [[ONIOM]] method,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chung |first1=Lung Wa |last2=Hirao |first2=Hajime |last3=Li |first3=Xin |last4=Morokuma |first4=Keiji |date=2012 |title=The ONIOM method: its foundation and applications to metalloenzymes and photobiology |url=https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wcms.85 |journal=WIREs Computational Molecular Science |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=327–350 |doi=10.1002/wcms.85 |s2cid=95472295 |issn=1759-0876|url-access=subscription }}</ref> a method that integrates molecular orbit methods and those of molecular mechanics at several levels and uses them to calculate large molecules.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Hirao |first1=Hajime |chapter=Chapter 8. Key Concepts and Applications of ONIOM Methods |date=2016 |chapter-url=http://ebook.rsc.org/?DOI=10.1039/9781782626831-00245 |title=Theoretical and Computational Chemistry Series |pages=245–293 |editor-last=Tunon |editor-first=Inaki |access-date=2023-10-27 |place=Cambridge |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry |doi=10.1039/9781782626831-00245 |isbn=978-1-78262-429-5 |last2=Xu |first2=Kai |last3=Chuanprasit |first3=Pratanphorn |last4=Moeljadi |first4=Adhitya Mangala Putra |last5=Morokuma |first5=Keiji |editor2-last=Moliner |editor2-first=Vicent|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> He investigated potential surfaces in chemical reactions and reactions and structure of nanoparticles, proteins and transition metal complexes as well as photochemistry of excited state molecules and biomolecules.<ref name=angchem /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morokuma |first=Keiji |date=2007-12-15 |title=Theoretical Studies of Chemical Reactions—A Fascinating World of Chemistry from Gas-Phase Elementary Reactions through Nanostructure Formation and Homogeneous Catalysis to Reactions of Metalloenzymes |journal=Bulletin of the Chemical Society of Japan |language=en |volume=80 |issue=12 |pages=2247–2261 |doi=10.1246/bcsj.80.2247 |issn=0009-2673|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=IAQMS />

== Honors and awards ==
Morokuma was a [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Sloan Research Fellow]] in 1970. In 1978, he received the Prize of the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]], of which he was a member. In 1991, he was the first to receive the [[Schrödinger Medal]]. In 1992 the Prize of the Japanese Chemical Society, in 2005 the Fukui Medal of the Asian Pacific Association of Theoretical & Computational Chemists and in 2008 the [[Imperial Prize of the Japan Academy]]. In 2009, he was recognized as the [[Person of Cultural Merit]] in Japan.<ref name=jpca /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Emory University News Release - keiji_morokuma_prize |url=https://www.emory.edu/news/Releases/keiji_morokuma_prize1206635753.html |access-date=2023-10-27 |website=www.emory.edu}}</ref>
